title: Depth-First Search
summary: Explore grids and choices as deep as possible with recursive and stack-based DFS, and backtrack to list every solution.
intro: Depth-first search follows one path as far as it goes, then backs up and tries the next. The same idea counts islands on a map, finds what a maze can reach, and lists every combination that fits a rule.

steps.title: Flood fill on a grid

example.title: Counting islands
example.prompt: Read a map of `#` land and `.` water and print how many islands it has and the size of each, in discovery order (row by row).
example.explanation: Each line becomes an array of characters, so `grid[r][c]` reads one cell. The double loop scans row by row, and every unvisited `#` it meets starts a new island. `islandSize` marks its cell, then for each offset it skips out-of-bounds neighbors first and recurses into unvisited land. Every call returns 1 plus what its neighbors found, so the first call returns the whole island's size. Visited cells are never counted again, so the scan finds each island once.

practice.title: Counting rooms
practice.prompt:
Read a floor plan of `.` floor and `#` walls and report how many rooms it has and how big the largest one is.

1. Turn the input lines into a grid of characters and build a visited grid of `false`.
2. Write `roomSize(r, c)`: a recursive DFS that marks floor cells visited and returns the size of the room. Only up, down, left, and right connect, never diagonals.
3. Start `roomSize` from every unvisited `.` cell and collect the sizes.
4. Print `Rooms: <count>`, then `Largest: <size>`, where the size is 0 when there are no rooms.

Input:

```text
########
#..#...#
#..#.#.#
####...#
#..#####
########
```

Expected output:

```text
Rooms: 3
Largest: 8
```
hints: Copy the shape of the island example and look for `.` instead of `#`.
Check `nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols` before you read `grid[nr][nc]`.
`Math.max(...sizes)` is `-Infinity` for an empty array, so write `Math.max(0, ...sizes)`.

steps.title: DFS with an explicit stack

example.title: Islands without recursion
example.prompt: Read a map of `#` land and `.` water and print how many islands it has and the size of each, using an explicit stack instead of recursion.
example.explanation: `islandSize` seeds the stack with the start cell and marks it visited. Each turn of the `while` loop pops one cell, counts it, and pushes its unvisited land neighbors, marking each as it is pushed so no cell enters the stack twice. When the stack is empty the island is done. The cells are visited in a different order than the recursive version, but the counts are identical, and no call stack grows however big the island is.

practice.title: Reachable from the start
practice.prompt:
Read a maze with one `S` and count the open cells you can reach from it, using a stack instead of recursion.

1. The starter already finds `S` at `startR`, `startC`, pushes it, and marks it visited.
2. While the stack is not empty, pop a cell and count it.
3. Push each in-bounds, unvisited neighbor that is not `#` (up, down, left, right), marking it visited when you push it.
4. Print `Reachable: <count>`, counting `S` itself.

Input:

```text
#######
#S..#.#
#.#.#.#
#.#...#
###.###
#...#.#
#######
```

Expected output:

```text
Reachable: 15
```
hints: The loop is the same as the one inside `islandSize` in the example. Only the test on the neighbor cell changes.
Any cell that is not `#` is open, including `S`, so test `grid[nr][nc] !== "#"`.
One test is a 150 by 150 maze, so a recursive version can overflow the call stack. Keep the `while` loop.

steps.title: Backtracking

example.title: Subsets under a limit
example.prompt: Read a limit and a line of increasing numbers and print every subset whose sum is at most the limit, in start-index order, then the total.
example.explanation: Every call saves a copy of `path`, so the empty subset comes first. The loop tries each remaining number from `start`: push it, explore with a bigger sum, then pop it. With `{1, 2}` the sum is 3, and adding 3 would make 6, so the loop breaks and also skips 4 without trying it. Because `i` starts at `start`, each subset appears once with its numbers in increasing order.

practice.title: Combinations that hit a target
hints: Follow the subsets example, but save `path` only when `sum === target`.
Use `results.push([...path])`. Pushing `path` itself leaves every saved entry empty at the end.
Values only grow, so once `sum + nums[i] > target` every later value is too big as well: `break`.

recap:
- Turn grid lines into arrays with `line.trim().split("")` and read cells as `grid[r][c]`.
- Walk neighbors with the offsets `[[1, 0], [-1, 0], [0, 1], [0, -1]]` and check bounds before reading a cell.
- Keep a boolean visited grid from `Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(false))` and mark a cell before exploring from it.
- Count regions by starting a DFS from every unvisited cell that belongs to one.
- Recursive DFS is short but limited by the call stack. An array stack with `push` and `pop` handles any size. Mark cells visited when you push them.
- Backtracking is choose, explore, un-choose. A loop from `start` builds each combination once in a fixed order.
- Save solutions with `[...path]`, and `break` early when sorted values make the rest of the loop hopeless.
